source: Moment of Inertia by Integration
I = ∫r² dm gives the rotational inertia of rods, rings, disks and spheres.
Students use the distance to the center of mass instead of the distance to the axis.

Rotational Inertia defined $I = \sum mr^2$ for point masses: mass far from the axis counts more. For a solid object, slice it into tiny pieces as in Center of Mass by Integration and add up $r^2\,dm$.

$$\role[moment of inertia]{mass}{I} = \int \role[distance from the axis]{position}{r}^2\,\role[tiny piece of mass]{mass}{dm},$$ where $r$ is each piece's distance from the axis of rotation. Results worth knowing: thin rod about its center $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, about one end $\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$; thin hoop $MR^2$; solid disk or cylinder about its axle $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$; solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$; thin spherical shell $\tfrac{2}{3}MR^2$.

Kinetic energy explains the $r^2$. A piece at distance $r$ moves at $v = r\omega$, so its energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}dm\,(r\omega)^2$. Adding over the body: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\int r^2\,dm\right)\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. Doubling a piece's distance from the axis doubles its speed and quadruples its energy at the same $\omega$.
A 2 m rod with $\lambda = 3x$ kg/m: $I$ about the light end is $\int_0^2 x^2(3x)\,dx = 12\ \text{kg·m}^2$.
Find $I$ for a uniform $2\ \text{kg}$ rod of length $1.2\ \text{m}$ about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod.
A uniform rod
$dm = \dfrac{M}{L}dx$ at distance $x$ from the end.
$I = \dfrac{M}{L}\int_0^L x^2\,dx = \dfrac{M}{L}\cdot\dfrac{L^3}{3} = \tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$.
$I = \tfrac{1}{3}(2)(1.2)^2 = 0.96\ \text{kg·m}^2$. (About the center it would be $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2 = 0.24\ \text{kg·m}^2$, a quarter as much.)
Show that a uniform disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ about its axle.
A solid disk from rings
Use rings: a ring of radius $r$ and width $dr$ has mass $dm = \sigma\,2\pi r\,dr$, with $\sigma = M/(\pi R^2)$, and all of it is at distance $r$.
$$I = \int_0^R r^2\,\sigma\,2\pi r\,dr = 2\pi\sigma\dfrac{R^4}{4} = \dfrac{M}{\pi R^2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi R^4}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$$

Two objects with the same mass and size can have very different $I$: a hoop puts all its mass at the rim ($MR^2$), a solid disk spreads it inward ($\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$). That difference decides races down ramps in Rolling Dynamics. For axes that don't pass through the center of mass, The Parallel-Axis Theorem saves you from integrating again.

Using each piece's distance from the center of mass, or from the middle of the object, when the axis is somewhere else. For a rod spinning about its end, the far end is a distance $L$ from the axis, not $L/2$. Check: draw the axis first and measure every $r$ from it. Also check the ranking: the same mass gives the largest $I$ when it sits farthest from the axis.
